gloss_terse: Hadadezer — the Aramean king of Zobah defeated by David; name means 'Hadad is (my) help'
gloss_readable: An Aramean royal name meaning 'Hadad is help,' borne by the king of Zobah whom David decisively defeated. The alternate spelling Hadarezer (found in Chronicles) reflects a scribal substitution of -r- for -d-, but ancient Aramaic inscriptions confirm Hadadezer as the original form. All 21 occurrences, whether preceded by prepositions or standing alone, refer to this single historical figure whose repeated clashes with Israel are narrated in 2 Samuel 8 and 10 and mirrored in 1 Chronicles 18-19.

senses.1: The proper name of the Aramean king of Zobah, son of Rehob, whose military forces David routed in campaigns recorded in 2 Samuel 8:3-12 and 10:16-19. Multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate the name (Hadadezer, Hadad-ezer, Hadadeser), and the LXX form Ἁδρααζαρ preserves a variant tradition. Also mentioned in 1 Kings 11:23 in connection with Rezon's earlier flight from Hadadezer's service.

gloss_terse: Zerubbabel — post-exilic governor of Judah who led the return from Babylon and rebuilt the Temple
gloss_readable: A name likely meaning 'offspring of Babylon,' pointing to the exile setting in which this leader was born. Zerubbabel led the first wave of returning exiles and oversaw the rebuilding of the Second Temple under prophetic encouragement from Haggai and Zechariah. Called 'governor of Judah' by Haggai and 'my servant' by the Lord, he occupies a pivotal place in post-exilic hope. His genealogy links him to the Davidic line through Shealtiel (or Pedaiah), keeping messianic expectations alive during the restoration.

senses.1: The personal name of the Davidic descendant who served as governor of Judah after the Babylonian exile. Grandson of King Jehoiachin, he appears in Ezra 2-4, Nehemiah 7 and 12, Haggai 1-2, and Zechariah 4. The Greek form Ζοροβαβελ is consistent across the LXX, and translations uniformly transliterate the name (Zerubabel, Zorobabel, Serubbabel), underscoring his singular identity in post-exilic literature.

gloss_terse: Zerah — 'rising, dawning'; name of several OT figures including a son of Judah and an Edomite chief
gloss_readable: A masculine name meaning 'rising' or 'dawning,' evocative of light breaking forth. Its most prominent bearer is the twin son of Judah and Tamar whose hand emerged first marked with a scarlet thread (Gen 38:30). The name is shared by at least five distinct individuals: an Edomite clan chief, a Cushite military leader who opposed Asa, two Levites in the Chronicles genealogies, and the head of a Simeonite family. Despite this variety, translations consistently render it as a simple transliteration.

senses.1: A proper name borne by multiple Old Testament figures, most notably the son of Judah and Tamar (Gen 38:30; 46:12), ancestor of a Judahite clan (Num 26:20; Josh 7:1). Also designates Edomite chiefs (Gen 36:13, 17, 33), Levitical ancestors (1 Chr 6:6, 26), a Simeonite clan head (Num 26:13), and a Cushite adversary of King Asa (2 Chr 14:8). Multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate (Zerach, Zera, Serach), and the LXX renders it Ζαρα or Ζαρε depending on the individual.

gloss_terse: Far be it! — an exclamation of strong repudiation, rejecting something as profane or abhorrent
gloss_readable: A forceful exclamation derived from the root meaning 'to profane,' literally something like 'to the profane place with that!' It expresses horrified rejection of a proposed action, functioning as a solemn oath of refusal. Abraham uses it twice when pleading with God over Sodom (Gen 18:25), Joseph's brothers invoke it to deny theft (Gen 44:7, 17), and David employs it when refusing to harm the Lord's anointed (1 Sam 26:11). Often strengthened by 'from the LORD' to underscore that the rejected act would violate divine order.

senses.1: An interjection expressing vehement moral or religious repudiation — 'far be it from me/you/us!' Constructed with the locative -ah ending on a root associated with profanation, it casts the contemplated action into the realm of the utterly unacceptable. Typically paired with a lamed of person and min-plus-infinitive of the deprecated act. Spanish 'lejos sea' and French 'loin être cela' capture the distancing force. Used in covenant contexts (Gen 44:17; Josh 24:16), royal self-restraint (1 Sam 26:11; 2 Sam 23:17), and theological argument (Gen 18:25; Job 27:5).

gloss_terse: Frankincense — the white aromatic resin burned in Israelite worship, grain offerings, and sacred incense
gloss_readable: The white aromatic resin harvested from Boswellia trees, named from the Hebrew root for 'white' on account of its pale color. Frankincense was a required component of the sacred incense blend (Exod 30:34) and accompanied grain offerings in the tabernacle and temple (Lev 2:1-16). It also appears in poetic imagery: the beloved in Song of Songs is associated with a hill of frankincense (4:6), and the prophets both celebrate and critique its ritual use (Isa 43:23; Jer 6:20). Cross-linguistic evidence is remarkably consistent, with cognates in Aramaic, Arabic, and Ethiopic all pointing to the same resin.

senses.1: The fragrant white resin of Boswellia trees, integral to Israelite cultic practice. Prescribed as one of four ingredients in the holy incense (Exod 30:34), it was placed on grain offerings (Lev 2:1, 15) and beside the showbread (Lev 24:7). Translations across languages converge: incienso (Spanish), encens (French), Weihrauch (German), لُبان (Arabic) — all pointing to the same aromatic substance. In Song of Songs 3:6 and 4:6, 14 it serves as a luxurious perfume image alongside myrrh.

gloss_terse: Scroll, written roll — a rolled document of parchment or papyrus used for recording prophecy and law
gloss_readable: The standard term for a written scroll in late biblical Hebrew, appearing almost exclusively in prophetic contexts. Its most dramatic appearance is in Jeremiah 36, where Baruch writes Jeremiah's oracles on a scroll that King Jehoiakim methodically cuts and burns — only for the prophet to dictate a replacement. Ezekiel receives a scroll written on both sides with lamentations (Ezek 2:9-3:3), and Zechariah sees a flying scroll of judgment (Zech 5:1-2). The Psalmist's reference to 'the scroll of the book' (Ps 40:7) links written text to covenantal obedience.

senses.1: A rolled document of papyrus or leather used for recording prophetic oracles, divine instructions, or other formal texts. Dominates the narrative of Jeremiah 36, where the noun occurs sixteen times as Baruch's scroll is written, read, confiscated, burned, and rewritten. Also designates the visionary scroll Ezekiel is commanded to eat (Ezek 2:9-3:3) and Zechariah's flying scroll of curse (Zech 5:1-2). Spanish 'rollo,' French 'rouleau,' and German 'Rolle' all preserve the physical sense of a rolled writing surface.

gloss_terse: Naomi — 'my delight, my pleasantness'; mother-in-law of Ruth, central figure in the book of Ruth
gloss_readable: A feminine name meaning 'my pleasantness' or 'my delight,' borne by the Bethlehemite woman whose story of loss and restoration frames the entire book of Ruth. After the deaths of her husband Elimelech and both sons in Moab, Naomi bitterly renames herself Mara ('bitter'), creating one of Scripture's most poignant wordplays on personal identity and divine providence. Her shrewd guidance of Ruth's actions leads to the marriage with Boaz and the birth of Obed, grandfather of David — making Naomi a quiet link in the messianic genealogy.

senses.1: The proper name of Ruth's mother-in-law, appearing exclusively in the book of Ruth (all 21 occurrences). The name itself means 'pleasant' or 'lovely,' which Naomi pointedly contrasts with Mara ('bitter') in Ruth 1:20 after her bereavement. Translations uniformly transliterate the name (Naomi, Noami, Noemí). She functions as the narrative architect whose return to Bethlehem, counsel to Ruth, and role as nurse to Obed (Ruth 4:16-17) tie the story together.

gloss_terse: Sisera — Canaanite commander under King Jabin of Hazor, defeated by Deborah and Barak; also a family name
gloss_readable: Primarily the name of the Canaanite military commander who led the forces of King Jabin of Hazor against Israel and was defeated through the combined agency of Deborah, Barak, and Jael (Judg 4-5). His nine hundred iron chariots symbolize overwhelming military power broken by divine intervention. Deborah's victory song in Judges 5 memorializes the scene of Sisera's mother waiting vainly for his return — one of the most vivid dramatic ironies in biblical poetry. A secondary Sisera appears as an ancestor of temple servants returning from exile (Ezra 2:53; Neh 7:55).

senses.1: The personal name of two distinct figures: primarily the Canaanite general under King Jabin defeated by Deborah and Barak at the Wadi Kishon (Judg 4:2-22; 5:20-30), killed by Jael with a tent peg, and recalled in later tradition (1 Sam 12:9; Ps 83:10); secondarily, the ancestor of a family of returning exiles (Ezra 2:53; Neh 7:55). The name may be of Hittite origin. Translations consistently transliterate as Sisera/Sísara across languages.

gloss_terse: Seren — lord, tyrant; the distinctive title for each of the five Philistine city-state rulers
gloss_readable: A loanword into Hebrew — likely from a pre-Semitic Aegean or Anatolian language — used exclusively for the rulers of the five Philistine city-states: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath. Unlike the broader Hebrew terms for 'king' or 'prince,' seren is a technical political title reserved for Philistine governance, appearing only in the plural. The word may be cognate with Greek tyrannos. These lords act collectively in key narratives: negotiating with Delilah against Samson (Judg 16), returning the captured ark (1 Sam 5-6), and rejecting David's service (1 Chr 12:20).

senses.1: The distinctive title for each of the five Philistine city-state rulers, always appearing in the plural (seranim). Used exclusively of Philistine political leadership in Joshua 13:3, Judges 3:3 and 16:5-30, 1 Samuel 5-7 and 29, and 1 Chronicles 12:20. The term functions as a loanword restricted to this one political context, never applied to Israelite or other rulers. Spanish 'príncipes,' German 'Herren,' and English 'lords' all approximate the sense of sovereign authority, though none captures the specifically Philistine connotation of the original.

gloss_terse: Asahel — 'God has made'; David's nephew famed for swiftness, also Levites and a post-exilic figure
gloss_readable: A theophoric name meaning 'God has made,' most famously borne by the swift-footed brother of Joab and Abishai and nephew of David. His fatal pursuit of Abner after the battle of Gibeon (2 Sam 2:18-23) and the blood-vengeance it triggered shaped the political tensions of David's early reign. He is listed among David's elite Thirty warriors (2 Sam 23:24; 1 Chr 11:26). The name also belongs to a Levite sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the law (2 Chr 17:8), a temple official under Hezekiah (2 Chr 31:13), and a post-exilic figure in Ezra 10:15.

senses.1: A proper name meaning 'God has made,' referring to at least four individuals: most prominently David's nephew, brother of Joab, renowned for being 'swift of foot as a wild gazelle' (2 Sam 2:18), whose death at Abner's hand provoked lasting enmity; also a Levitical teacher under Jehoshaphat (2 Chr 17:8), a temple administrator under Hezekiah (2 Chr 31:13), and a post-exilic contemporary of Ezra (Ezra 10:15). The LXX form Ασαηλ and multilingual glosses (Asahel, Asael, Asah) consistently transliterate the name.
